definition: Running a trained model to produce outputs (answers, code, images). Unlike training it is continuous, latency-sensitive and priced per token.
The first phase of an inference request: the whole prompt is processed in parallel to build the KV cache and produce the first token. Compute-bound.
The second phase of an inference request: output tokens are produced one at a time, each requiring a full read of the model's weights. Memory-bandwidth-bound.
The keys and values of every earlier token, stored in GPU memory so attention does not recompute them. Grows with context length and number of users; often the binding memory constraint in serving.
An attention design in which several query heads share one key/value head, shrinking the KV cache (8x for Llama 3.1 70B) with little quality loss.
DeepSeek's attention design that caches a small compressed latent vector per token instead of full keys and values, cutting KV-cache memory by over 90%.
Serving many requests in the same GPU step so one read of the weights is shared by all of them. Raises throughput per GPU but slows each individual user.
Scheduling at every generation step so requests can join and leave a running batch, instead of waiting for the whole batch to finish. Standard in modern serving engines.
A technique (from vLLM) that stores the KV cache in fixed-size pages like virtual memory, avoiding fragmentation and letting requests share cached prefixes.
How long a user waits between sending a request and seeing the first token. Driven mainly by prefill compute and queueing.

term: TPOT / ITL (time per output token / inter-token latency)
definition: The gap between successive streamed tokens; 1/TPOT is tokens per second per user. Driven mainly by decode bandwidth and batch size.
The curve of best achievable tokens/s per GPU (throughput) at each tokens/s per user (interactivity). Hardware and software generations are compared by how far they push the whole curve.
Storing and computing with fewer bits per number (e.g. FP8 or FP4 instead of BF16). Cuts memory and bandwidth per token, at some risk to accuracy.
NVIDIA's 4-bit floating-point format for Blackwell and Rubin: 4-bit values with an FP8 scale per block of 16 plus a per-tensor scale, about 4.5 bits per value in total.
FLOPs performed per byte moved from memory. Work below a chip's ratio of peak FLOPS to memory bandwidth (its ridge point) is memory-bound; decode at small batch sizes is far below it.
A small draft model proposes several tokens and the large model verifies them in one pass, keeping the correct ones. Produces identical output 2-3x faster when decode is memory-bound.
Running prefill and decode on separate pools of GPUs and transferring the KV cache between them, so each pool can be sized and tuned for its own bottleneck.
A model trained (usually with reinforcement learning) to generate a hidden chain of thought before answering. Better answers on hard problems at the cost of many more generated tokens.
Spending more inference computation per query (longer reasoning, multiple attempts, search) to get a better answer, rather than training a bigger model.
Systems in which a model plans, calls tools, reads results and iterates over many steps to complete a task. One task can consume hundreds of model calls and millions of tokens.
